quote_orig: Cumq; multi inde loquerentur, & testificarentur, maximeq; Mufatha & Hazen, ad ultimum vero Hali filius Abitalib princeps & nobilis inter suos inde eum liberius argueret, copiam mulierum esse dices, nec decere tantum hominem a muliercula dehonestari, dignamq; repudio esse confirmaret, respondit, nullam sibi adeo charam vel dilectam, utpote quam virginem acceperat, & adhuc iuuenculam.
own_translation_en: Many people spoke about this and testified, and especially Mufatha and Hazen; at last Ali son of Abu Talib, a prince and noble among his people, argued against him more freely, saying he had an abundance of women and that it was not fitting for so great a man to be dishonoured by a little woman, and maintained that she deserved repudiation; he answered that he had no one so dear or beloved to him, since he had taken her as a virgin and still a young girl.
licence_note: The 1550 Latin is public domain (16th century). The archive.org scan carries 'All rights reserved by the Newberry Library': only the words are quoted; no image is reproduced. No PD English translation exists (the only English version, Londini Ensis 2010, is in copyright and was NOT quoted); the English above is the team's own literal translation.
what_it_says: In this polemic, Ali son of Abu Talib presses Muhammad to put away a wife, and Muhammad answers that he loves her above all because he took her as a virgin and still a young girl. Youth is only implied here; no number is given.
context: The passage follows a narrative about Muhammad's wife Ayffa (Aisha) and an alleged affair; the author presents it as part of the moral charges against Muhammad's lust. The Latin is a 16th-century back-translation of a Greek translation of Riccoldo's Latin, so the wording is not Riccoldo's own, and the attribution rests on the title page plus the match with the 1606 printing.
limits: Youth is implied ('virgin, still young'), not stated as an age. The sentences around the quote contain the affair accusation, which is deliberately left out of the quotation. The author is a polemicist reporting a story, not a neutral witness. The passage is absent from the 1606 printing (checked in the PDF text layer, pp. 40-130). The 1550 section boundaries beyond the title page were not verified. Translation from Greek makes the exact Latin uncertain at the level of word choice.
stance: own view (polemic) reporting a Muslim story

url: https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_u0DM9SzvBlMC (PDF p. 49; page image read at 400 dpi)
quote_orig: Duae autem ex vxoribus Mahometi, quarum altera quidem dicebatur Aiefe, filia Empipecer, aliarum nobilissima: altera autem Aafa, filia Omar, mouebantur zelotipia in Mariam.
own_translation_en: Two of Muhammad's wives, of whom one was called Aiefe, daughter of Empipecer, the most noble of the others, and the other Aafa, daughter of Omar, were moved to jealousy of Mary.
licence_note: archive.org metadata: Public Domain Mark 1.0 (Google Books 1606 scan). No PD English translation; own literal translation given. 'Empipecer' is as printed (probably Abubacer / Abu Bakr; not resolved here). 'Aafa' is as printed (Hafsa).
what_it_says: The Confutatio names Muhammad's wife Aiefe, daughter of Empipecer (Abu Bakr), as jealous of his concubine Mary, together with Hafsa; it presents the jealousy as part of his lustful and deceitful conduct.
context: The sentence opens the Mary story (Muhammad sleeping with a concubine, the wives' complaint, and a Qur'anic revelation at Surah 66 that he uses to justify his oath-breaking). The author's aim is to show that the law is a product of lust and deceit.
limits: No age is given for any wife. The sentence is the author's narrative of a Muslim story, not a Muslim source's own words. Concubine affair is only reported, not described. Aiefe is named as one of the jealous wives, not as the target of the criticism. Printed spelling of the name is 'Aiefe' (not 'Aisha'); the mapping to Aisha rests on the father's name and the context.
stance: own view (polemic) reporting a Muslim story

url: https://archive.org/details/case_bp127_l3_1550 (PDF p. 272; page image read at 300 dpi)
quote_orig: Dixit etiam Aiffa uxor Machumet, Hali multa inde abstulisse, & pene totum demutasse, & insuper prohibuisse homines, ne legeretur Alchoran, & propter hoc multos sepe uerberasse.
own_translation_en: Aiffa, the wife of Muhammad, is also said to have said that Ali took much from it, altered almost all of it, and moreover forbade people to read the Qur'an, and for this reason often beat many people.
licence_note: 1550 text public domain; scan 'All rights reserved by the Newberry Library' (words quoted, not images). No PD English translation found; own literal translation.
what_it_says: The dossier reports a Muslim tradition in which Aisha, Muhammad's wife, accuses Ali of having altered much of the Qur'an and of having banned its reading. The Latin reports, but does not endorse, the claim.
context: The passage is in the Latin dossier's section on how the Qur'an was collected and then dispersed; the text reports a variety of Muslim traditions on the Qur'anic text. The Arabic source is not identified in this pass.
limits: This is a Muslim tradition about the Qur'an's text, not about the marriage; no criticism of the marriage and no age. The Latin is a 12th-century translation from Arabic; the Arabic source and its date are unknown here. The name 'Aiffa' is a print spelling read from the image; the long-s glyph is ambiguous but reads as ff.

quote_orig: Probant & hoc plura quae circa mulieres permisit. Vt illud Capite III. Mulieres vobis subiectas penitus, pro modo vestro ubicunque volueritis parate. Et Capite VIII. tot permittit uxores, quot quaerit quisque subiugare, seu castigare.
own_translation_en: They prove this also by many other things that he permitted concerning women. As in that passage in chapter 3: Women subject to you, prepare them as you wish wherever you want. And in chapter 8: he permits as many wives as each one wishes to subjugate or chastise.
licence_note: 1550 text public domain; scan rights as above. No PD English translation; own literal translation. 'Capitulum' numbers refer to the Qur'an in Latin (Robert of Ketton's numbering), not to Cusanus.
keys: tot permittit uxores, quot quaerit quisque subiugare
Probant & hoc plura quae circa mulieres permisit
what_it_says: Cusanus says the Qur'an permits a man as many wives as he wishes, and that Muhammad's law thereby indulges lust. He quotes the Latin Qur'an, not any Aisha passage.
context: Liber secundus of the Cribratio tests the Qur'an's law against Christian and Jewish law; this passage belongs to his critique of the law's sexual permissions.
limits: Generic: names no wife, gives no age, does not mention Aisha. The team's rule is that the number of wives is not a criticism of Aisha's age; this passage is included only to document the 1461 Latin critique of polygamy. Verified by page image; the Qur'an quotations are Cusanus' Latin renderings.

quote_orig: Luxuriosus & bellicosus fuit: idcoque de immunditia & vanitate legem tulit; quam carnaliter viuentes in parte voluptatis firmiter obiiciunt.
own_translation_en: He was lustful and warlike; therefore he gave a law about impurity and vanity, which people who live carnally firmly hold to, in the part that concerns pleasure.
licence_note: Public domain (1611). OCR text layer only; the OCR is poor in this line (e.g. 'lmmunditia', 'obieiwant'), so the quote is LOW RELIABILITY and needs a page-image check before use. Own literal translation.
what_it_says: Vitry calls Muhammad lustful and warlike and says his law about impurity and vanity suits people who live for carnal pleasure.
context: The sentence is in Vitry's brief opening account of Muhammad, which describes him as illiterate, a heretic taught by a monk (Sergius) and a warlike leader who spread his law by the sword.
limits: No Aisha, no wife, no age. Generic lust only; included to document the early 13th-century criticism of Muhammad's character, not of Aisha's age. OCR only, not checked against the page image. Printed page not determined.
